title: Helix Bio — POC scoping: latency SLOs and benchmarks
summary: POC scoping focused on defining latency and throughput SLOs (TTFT vs TPOT), workload sizing for a bioinformatics summarization feature, benchmark plan, and timeline. Agreed on target interactive SLOs and measurement approach with warm/cold cache splits; next steps include sending bench scripts, sample queries, and scheduling runs.
topics: p95/p99 targets for interactive and batch use-cases
workload sizing (qps, concurrency, avg token output)
transcript:
[00:00] Ava (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're here to scope the POC for the summarization feature and nail down latency SLOs and the bench plan
[00:12] Maya (Helix CTO): yep thanks Ava, we want to validate that this can run with sub-200ms first byte for the interactive UI and that cost is reasonable, so trying to get clear numbers
[00:25] Diego (Redwood SE): cool, quick intro from our side — Diego on infra/perf, Lina will help design the bench harness; we'll walk through TTFT vs TPOT and proposed targets, then talk measurement plan
[00:40] Jonas (Helix Lead ML Eng): to set context, our feature takes 500–1,200 token inputs (DNA+annotations) and returns ~150–300 token summaries. Peak qps expected 35–50 during business hours, steady 10–15 qps, spikes to 100 qps occasionally.
[01:05] Ava: got it. two common SLOs we use: TTFT — time to first token (time from request to first emitted token), and TPOT — time per output token (avg time to generate each subsequent token). important to separate since first token can be dominated by model load/warmup and routing, whereas TPOT reflects per-token throughput when streaming
[01:30] Priya (IT Security): quick note — our security team needs to see SOC2, encryption at rest, KMS integration, and a VPC option. will the POC use private networking?
[01:45] Lina: we can run the POC against Redwood Private in a VPC or a hosted dedicated pool; for the benchmark we recommend a dedicated pool to avoid noisy neighbor variance unless you want to exercise hosted variability
[02:05] Evan (SRE): variance matters — we want both warm and cold-start numbers. cold starts simulate scaled-up nodes or model swap.
[02:18] Diego: agreed. proposed measurement plan: 1) cold TTFT: empty KV/prefix cache, route new model instance; 2) warm TTFT: warmed caches and warmed kernels; 3) sustained TPOT: steady-state token generation at target concurrency; 4) spike/resilience: step load to 2–3x expected qps to see degradation/fallback. we'll capture p50/p95/p99 for each slice
[02:49] Maya: what should our numeric targets be? we mentioned sub-200ms for TTFT earlier
[02:55] Ava: for interactive summarization I'd propose p95 TTFT <= 250ms and p99 <= 450ms for the warm case; for cold TTFT p95 <= 700ms and p99 <= 1.2s — those are ambitious but reasonable with quantized weights and a dedicated pool. For TPOT, aim for p95 per-token time < 35ms (which maps to ~28 tokens/sec), p99 < 70ms per token for warm steady-state.
[03:32] Jonas: that p95 TPOT number — how does that translate to end-to-end for a 200-token summary?
[03:38] Diego: multiply roughly: 200 tokens * 35ms = 7s for streaming generation after first token; add TTFT for first token, so interactive feel depends on streaming UX — we can also use chunked responses to show partial top-level summary faster.
[03:58] Maya: 7s is borderline for our UX. can we trade TPOT for cost/accuracy? i.e., smaller model or distillation?
[04:06] Ava: yes — trade-offs: smaller models reduce TTFT and TPOT but may drop summary quality. Redwood Optimize can suggest model/quantization profiles per prompt set; we should run evals on your sample prompts to see quality delta.
[04:22] Priya: also want to understand p99 tail causes, like KV cache misses, model paging, or infra congestion. we need the bench to surface root causes, not just numbers
[04:33] Lina: we'll instrument bench to tag requests as cache-warm vs cache-cold, note CPU/GPU mem pressure, kernel fallback, and measure router latency separately. logs/traces will be captured and shared.
[04:50] Evan: do you support measuring per-token latency breakdown? e.g., kernel time vs serialization vs network?
[04:55] Diego: yes — runtime exposes token-level timing hooks and we can emit traces per token; we'll include that in the bench harness output CSV/JSON. note that network serialization can be minimized by colocating runner and client in same VPC during private POC
[05:12] Maya: about workload sizing — we'll provide real qps distributions and a sample of 1k queries. Jonas will send the 1k dataset.
[05:20] Jonas: i'll prepare the sample and include token lengths and expected concurrency profile; also i can run a local baseline on our current setup (self-hosted smaller model) so we have a delta
[05:30] Ava: timeline suggestion: we send bench scripts + infra config 48 hours after call, Helix wires up credentials and dataset in 3 business days, dry run next week, full run the week after. does that work?
[05:44] Maya: yes that's fine, our security guys need the SOC2 docs before opening access but we can provision a scoped VPC account and keys once we see the security packet
[05:56] Priya: please include key rotation details and KMS integration notes in the security packet
[06:02] Diego: noted. on measurement specifics:
[06:06] [06:06] Diego: we'll run the following metrics per test slice: request latency (TTFT), token latency (TPOT), tokens/sec throughput, GPU utilization, queue depths, and error rates. each test will run long enough to reach steady-state — 5–10 minutes at stable qps, and 10–15 minutes for spike tests
[06:28] Lina: bench harness specifics: uses k6 + custom client for streaming, supports replaying your real queries with original tokenization, simulates concurrency distribution, supports prefix caching toggles, and will output p50/p95/p99 with histograms and raw traces
[06:45] Jonas: what's your recommendation on model variant for the POC? we have two candidates: a 30B open model and a distilled 7B.
[06:53] Ava: for quality check, run both. POC bench should include: 1) 7B distilled for baseline TTFT/TPOT/cost; 2) 30B quantized (4-bit) for quality and perf; measure tradeoffs. Redwood can suggest quant profiles.
[07:08] Maya: what about cold-start frequency in production — our ops team scales nodes dynamically so cold conditions are realistic
[07:15] Evan: we'll give you our autoscale policy; bench should trigger cold starts by spinning nodes down between runs for certain tests
[07:24] Lina: we'll parameterize the bench to force model reloads and to clear KV caches between iterations; results will be labeled cold/warm in the report
[07:33] Ava: acceptance criteria proposal (we should capture this as success criteria):
[07:38] Ava: - Functionality: model outputs meet our quality threshold on sample evals (Jonas to define pass rate)
[07:44] Ava: - Latency SLOs (warm): TTFT p95 <= 250ms, p99 <= 450ms; TPOT p95 per token < 35ms, p99 < 70ms
[07:55] Ava: - Cold-start tolerances: TTFT p95 <= 700ms, p99 <= 1.2s
[08:02] Ava: - Throughput: sustain 50 qps with <= 5% error rate and GPU utilization <= 80% for the chosen instance type
[08:12] Maya: those look good as a starting point. if the 30B can't meet them we'll look at a hybrid: small model for quick interactive, larger model async for deep summaries
[08:23] Priya: and security acceptance: SOC2 docs provided, KMS integration verified, VPC connectivity tested
[08:29] Diego: reporting plan: we'll provide a bench report with p50/p95/p99 tables, histograms, token-level traces, GPU metrics, and root-cause notes for tail events. we'll also include a recommended config (batching, quant, instance type) and estimated cost per 1M tokens for both models
[08:47] Jonas: good — on cost, include per-minute and per-token approximations and how batching affects unit economics
[08:53] Ava: next steps recap — we'll send bench scripts and security packet; Helix shares dataset and creds; then schedule dry run; then run full suite and share results + recommended configs
[09:08] Maya: ok can you email the security packet to priya@helixbio.com and the bench plan to ops@helixbio.com?
[09:14] Ava: yes will do. any other questions?
[09:18] Evan: one small ask — can you include any known regressions or model id mismatches in the report if they happen? we need traceability for audits
[09:25] Lina: we'll include model versioning and hashes in the report, along with logs for reproducibility
[09:32] Ava: excellent. thanks everyone, we'll follow up with timing.
[09:36] Maya: thanks all
[09:38] [meeting ends]
